summary: This memo defines an NNTP extension for streaming, or asynchronous, transfer of articles between servers, which is much more efficient than the older approach. It formalizes the CHECK and TAKETHIS commands from RFC 2980 and deprecates the MODE STREAM command.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of asking whether a friend wants each letter one at a time and waiting, you keep sending offers and letters without stopping. News servers share posts much faster this way.

questions: what do check and takethis do in nntp
subtitle: How news servers pipeline article offers and transfers with CHECK and TAKETHIS instead of waiting on every IHAVE.

tldr.problem: The NNTP IHAVE command cannot be pipelined, so a server must stop and wait for each answer before offering the next article, which greatly limits throughput.
tldr.mechanism: The STREAMING extension splits IHAVE into CHECK (is this article wanted?) and TAKETHIS (here it is). Both can be pipelined, and they use distinct response codes so replies can be told apart.
tldr.outcome: Servers can spend far more of their time moving articles. The RFC formalizes the ad-hoc CHECK and TAKETHIS commands from RFC 2980, updates that RFC, and deprecates MODE STREAM.

today: RFC 4644 is a Proposed Standard and is not marked as obsoleted or updated by any other RFC. It updates RFC 2980 by formalizing CHECK and TAKETHIS and deprecating MODE STREAM.

sections.title: Why Streaming Feeds
sections.content:
Under the base NNTP specification (RFC 3977), a peer uses IHAVE to ask whether a server wants a particular article. Because IHAVE cannot be pipelined, the need to wait for each response greatly restricts throughput.

The ad-hoc CHECK and TAKETHIS commands, first documented in RFC 2980, offer a more effective use of bandwidth. Because of their proven usefulness and wide deployment, this RFC formalizes them. It also deprecates the ad-hoc MODE STREAM command, but documents it for backwards compatibility.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking about each article and waiting wastes time, like asking permission for every single toy before moving it. This RFC lets servers ask and send in big batches.

sections.title: How Streaming Transfer Works
sections.content:
The STREAMING extension gives the same function as IHAVE but splits the query and the transfer into CHECK and TAKETHIS. Both can be pipelined. A streaming client will often pipeline many CHECK commands, use the answers to build a list of wanted articles, and then send them with a pipelined sequence of TAKETHIS commands.

The two commands use distinct response codes, so they can be mixed in one pipeline and the client can still tell which command each response belongs to.

A client MAY send an article with TAKETHIS without a prior CHECK, but SHOULD NOT do this for every article unless the site administrator configured it so from out-of-band information. A client MAY adapt: start with CHECK for everything, switch to bare TAKETHIS when most articles are accepted (over 95% might be a reasonable metric), and switch back if the acceptance rate falls much below that.
sections.plainLanguage: First you hold up a list of things and ask which ones are wanted. Then you hand over just those. If nearly everything is always wanted, you can skip asking.

sections.title: Advertising Support and MODE STREAM
sections.content:
A server that supports streaming advertises the STREAMING capability in response to CAPABILITIES. It MUST keep advertising it after a client issues MODE STREAM, and MAY advertise it before and after MODE READER with the same meaning.

MODE STREAM was historically how a client discovered support. It is now deprecated in favor of CAPABILITIES. New clients SHOULD use CAPABILITIES but MAY use MODE STREAM with legacy servers, and servers MUST accept it for legacy clients. A supporting server returns 203 (or 501 if an argument is given). Despite its name it does not change server state, so it MAY be pipelined, and a server MUST NOT require it before accepting CHECK or TAKETHIS.

The RFC notes that MODE STREAM may be removed from a future version of the specification, so clients are urged to move to CAPABILITIES.
sections.plainLanguage: A server puts up a sign saying 'I do streaming.' The old way was knocking and asking; the sign is now the polite way, though servers still answer the knock.

sections.title: The CHECK and TAKETHIS Commands
sections.content:
CHECK message-id tells the server the client has that article. The server answers 238 if it wants a copy, 438 if it does not (for example it already has it), or 431 if it is not wanted right now and the client should retry later. Each response repeats the client's message-id. These answers are advisory, and the server MUST NOT rely on the client to behave as they request.

TAKETHIS message-id is followed immediately by the whole article, headers and body, as a multi-line data block ended by a single dot on a line. The server answers 239 if the article was transferred or 439 if it was rejected. On a temporary error it MUST reply 400 and close the connection.

A client MUST NOT use TAKETHIS unless the server advertises STREAMING or returned 203 to MODE STREAM. Unlike POST, it is for forwarding already-posted articles between hosts and SHOULD NOT be used by personal news readers. The client SHOULD NOT assume success without an affirmative response, and a dropped connection, timeout or 400 SHOULD be treated as a temporary failure. A server MAY send 239 and later silently discard the article.
sections.plainLanguage: CHECK is 'do you want this one?' with the answers yes, no, or ask me later. TAKETHIS is 'here it is,' and the server says got it or no thanks.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content: Section 3 gives ABNF that extends the base NNTP grammar. It adds CHECK and TAKETHIS followed by a message-id, and MODE STREAM. It adds the article data stream of TAKETHIS, the response lines 238, 239, 431, 438 and 439 with a message-id, and the capability entry STREAMING. The base NNTP ABNF should be imported first before validating these rules.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the exact spelling guide for the new commands and replies, so every server writes them the same way.

sections.title: Security and Registry Notes
sections.content:
The RFC says that no new security considerations are introduced beyond those in the core NNTP specification.

For the IANA registry it defines the STREAMING extension: the capability label is STREAMING with no arguments, and it defines three new commands. It does not change existing commands, command or response line length, or pipelining, and it does not alter the capabilities list. Using MODE READER on a mode-switching server may disable the extension.
sections.plainLanguage: It adds no new safety worries beyond regular news serving, and it fills out the official registry form for the new feature.
